pass_a_gloss: Matthew's pre-prayer sayings frame prayer against ambition: hypocrites' street-corner theater, closet secrecy, heathen wordiness. Vainglory pollutes even good deeds; Jesus' oath-backed 'they have received their reward' parallels the rich man's exhausted good things and the flesh-sower's corruption. The broad way is all corners; pleasure-lovers get drunk on prayer itself, fallen from the unbending narrow way.
pass_b_english: Since, as we said in what went before, the one who prays must first be established — how disposed and in what condition — and only then pray, let us see, before the prayer that lies in Matthew, the words spoken about it by our Savior, which run thus: 'When you pray, you shall not be as the hypocrites; for they love to pray standing in the synagogues and on the corners of the streets, that they may be seen by men. Amen, I say to you: they have received their reward. But thou, when thou prayest, enter into thy closet, and shut thy door, and pray to thy Father who is in secret; and thy Father who sees in secret shall repay thee. And when you pray, do not babble as the heathen do; for they think that in their much speaking they shall be heard. Be not like them, then; for your Father knows what need you have before you ask him. Pray, then, like this.' (Matthew 6:5–9)

In many places, then, our Savior is seen pressing against ambition as a passion that destroys; which he has done here also, turning men away from performing a hypocrite's work at the season of prayer. For it is a hypocrite's work to want to preen oneself before men for piety or for fellowship. But we must remember the 'How can you believe, who receive glory from men, and seek not the glory that comes from the only God?' (John 5:44) — and despise all glory from men, even if it is thought to come of the good — and seek the sovereign and true glory, the glory from the only God, who becomingly glorifies, beyond the worth of the glorified, the one worthy of glory. Even what was thought good and praiseworthy is polluted when deemed to be done — when we do it 'that we may be glorified by men' or 'that we may be seen by men.' That is why no recompense from God follows upon it. For every word of Jesus is unlying — and, if one must force the saying, becomes more unlying still when spoken with his customary oath. He says of those who do good for show to win human glory, or who pray 'in the synagogues and on the corners of the streets' (Luke 16:25) 'that they may be seen by men,' the same thing: 'Amen, I say to you: they have received their reward.' (Galatians 6:8) For as the rich man in Luke 'received his good things' in his human 'life' — and, having drawn them off, has no more room to receive them after this present life — so he who draws off 'his reward' for himself, whether in giving to someone or in prayers, as one who sowed 'not to the Spirit' but 'to the flesh,' shall 'reap corruption' indeed, but shall not 'reap eternal life.' He sows 'to the flesh' who, 'in the synagogues and in the streets, that' (Matthew 6:2) he may be glorified 'by men,' gives 'alms' with a trumpet 'before' himself, or who, loving 'to pray standing in the synagogues and on the corners of the streets, that,' (Matthew 7:13) having been seen 'by men,' he may be reputed by the onlookers to be some pious and holy man.

But everyone who walks the broad and roomy way that leads away 'to destruction' — which has nothing straight or direct, but is all crooked and cornered (for it is rent by 'corners,' in which 'men' who, dying because they have fallen from divinity, 'glorify and bless' those reputed among them to be impious in the streets) — and many there always are who appear in prayer to be lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God, getting drunk on prayer in the midst of banquets and beside wine, truly 'standing on the corners of the streets' and praying. For everyone who lives for pleasure, loving the roomy way, has fallen out of the narrow and straitened way of Jesus Christ, which has not even a chance bend, and is nowhere at all cornered.
